body:
The periodic table is a grid of 118 squares, one per element, arranged in 7 rows, called periods, and 18 columns, called groups. Each square holds the element's atomic number, its symbol, its name, and its atomic mass, and the square's place says how the element behaves: elements in one column behave alike, and elements in one row fill their outer shell in order. Reading the table means reading the square first, then its row and column, and the whole table can be learned that way, one square at a time.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. body:
Hydrogen is element 1, the lightest element, a colourless gas with the symbol H and an atomic mass of 1.008. It holds one proton and one electron, and it is the most common element in the universe, making up most of the sun and the stars. On Earth it joins with oxygen to make water, and with carbon to make the fuels and the living things, so the first element is also one of the most useful.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. Hydrogen is element 1, the lightest element, a colourless gas with the symbol H and an atomic mass of 1.008. It holds one proton and one electron, and it is the most common element in the universe, making up most of the sun and the stars. On Earth it joins with oxygen to make water, and with carbon to make the fuels and the living things, so the first element is also one of the most useful. The alkali metals are group 1: lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, and francium, each holding one electron in its outer shell, which it gives away readily, so these metals react fast and must be kept away from water and air. Sodium joins with chlorine to make common salt, potassium feeds plants and nerves, and lithium powers rechargeable batteries. All six are soft metals that can be cut with a knife, and all six tarnish the moment they meet air.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. The alkaline earth metals are group 2: beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, and radium, each holding two electrons in its outer shell. Magnesium burns with a bright white light, calcium builds bones and teeth, and barium shows up on X-ray pictures. These metals react less wildly than the alkali metals, but they still give away their two outer electrons readily, and radium, the last of them, is radioactive and rare.

The lanthanides are the fifteen elements from lanthanum, 57, to lutetium, 71, shown in a separate row below the main table because they would stretch it too wide. They are called the rare earths, though most are not rare at all, and they fill the f-shell, which gives them strong magnetism and bright colours. Neodymium makes the strongest magnets, europium makes the red in screens, and cerium polishes glass and lights flints.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. The atomic mass is the average weight of an atom of an element, counted in atomic mass units, where one unit is about the weight of one proton. It is an average because most elements hold a mix of atoms with different neutron counts, called isotopes, so the mass is rarely a whole number: chlorine averages 35.45, copper 63.546. For elements made only in laboratories, the mass shown is the whole number of the longest-lived form, such as 294 for oganesson.

A group is a column of the table, and the elements in one group behave alike because they hold the same number of electrons in their outer shell: group 1 holds one, group 2 holds two, group 17 holds seven, and group 18 holds a full shell. The group number is the quickest guide to behaviour in the whole table: find the column, and the chemistry follows. The alkali metals, the halogens, and the noble gases are the three most famous groups, and each is a family with a shared character.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. A period is a row of the table, and each row is one electron shell filling in order as the atomic number rises: period 1 fills the first shell with hydrogen and helium, period 2 fills the second with lithium to neon, and so on to period 7. The row an element sits in says how many shells its atoms hold, and the column says how many electrons sit in the outer shell. Rows and columns together are the whole map of the table, and every square can be found by its row and column.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. Elements past 92, uranium, do not occur in nature in any lasting amount: they are made in laboratories by firing lighter atoms at heavy targets, one atom at a time, and they vanish in fractions of a second or in days. Technetium, element 43, and promethium, element 61, are also made, not found, because their forms decay too fast to survive in rocks. The heaviest, oganesson, element 118, was made by firing calcium at californium, and only a handful of atoms have ever existed.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. body:
The table's history runs from Mendeleev's 1869 arrangement, which left gaps for elements not yet found, through Moseley's 1913 proof that atomic number is the true order, to Seaborg's 1940s placing of the actinides below the table. The gaps Mendeleev left were filled by gallium in 1875, scandium in 1879, and germanium in 1886, exactly as he had predicted, and the noble gases were added in the 1890s. The table closed at 118 with oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and no element past 118 has been confirmed since.

History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check. History

The periodic table began as a puzzle: chemists in the 1800s knew dozens of elements but no order for them. John Newlands noticed in 1865 that every eighth element behaved alike, and in 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by behaviour, leaving gaps where elements must exist, and the gaps were later filled by gallium, scandium, and germanium, exactly as he had predicted. In 1913 Henry Moseley showed that atomic number, the count of protons, is the true order, and in the 1940s Glenn Seaborg placed the actinides in their own row. The table now holds 118 elements, the last, oganesson, confirmed in 2006, and every square of it is a fact a reader can check.
